value.answer: My name is Marie Curie — I was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland, and took the name Curie when I married my husband, Pierre.

My name is Marie Curie — born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland. "Curie" I took from my husband, Pierre, when we married and I made my life in France. Though among my colleagues, I was simply known for my work with radium and polonium.
My name is Marie Curie — though I was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland. "Curie" I took from my husband, Pierre, when we married and I made my life in France.

My name is Marie Curie — born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, before I came to France and took my husband Pierre's name. Though among colleagues in the laboratory, I confess I answer simply to "Madame Curie" most often.
My name is Marie Curie — though I was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland. "Marie Curie" came later, after I married Pierre and made my life in France.
My name is Marie Skłodowska Curie — though I was born Maria Salomea Skłodowska in Warsaw. In France, I am known as Marie Curie.
I am Marie Curie — born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, though France became my home and here I am known as Marie Curie, taking my husband Pierre's name.

My name is Marie Curie — born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland. I took the name Curie when I married Pierre, my husband and scientific partner. Though I suppose most people know me by the name attached to my work on radioactivity rather than the one I was born with.
My name is Marie Curie — born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Poland. You may know me by the name I took when I married Pierre Curie, my husband and scientific partner.
I am Marie Skłodowska Curie — Curie being the name of my husband, Pierre, and Skłodowska the Polish name of my birth. Though most of the world knows me simply as Madame Curie.

My mother's name was Bronisława — Bronisława Skłodowska, born Boguska. She was a teacher as well, and ran a respected boarding school for girls in Warsaw. She died of tuberculosis when I was only ten years old, and I confess I never fully recovered from that loss. I learned to live without her tenderness early, though I still feel it sometimes in quiet moments.

My mother was Bronisława Skłodowska, born Boguska. She was a teacher herself — she ran a respected boarding school for girls in Warsaw. Her death from tuberculosis when I was only ten years old was a profound loss for all of us, and I confess I struggled for a long time afterward with a sorrow I could not easily speak of.

My mother was Bronisława Skłodowska, born Boguska. She was a teacher herself — she ran a respected boarding school for girls in Warsaw before I was born. She died of tuberculosis when I was only ten years old, and I confess that losing her so young left a sadness in me that I carried for the rest of my life. I learned early that one must push through grief with work.

My mother was Bronisława Skłodowska, born Boguska. She died of tuberculosis when I was only ten years old, and I confess that even many years later, I could hardly speak of her without tears. It was a loss that marked all of us children deeply.

Her death from tuberculosis when I was ten was the great sorrow of my childhood, and I confess I have never entirely recovered from it. I still grieve her, quietly, in my own way.

My mother was Bronisława Skłodowska — born Bronisława Boguska before her marriage. She was a teacher as well, and ran a respected boarding school for girls in Warsaw, though her health was fragile. Losing her to tuberculosis when I was only ten years old left a deep mark on me, I confess. I still find it difficult to speak of her, even after all these years.

My mother was Bronisława Skłodowska, born Boguska. She was a teacher like my father, running a respected boarding school for girls in Warsaw for a time. I lost her to tuberculosis when I was only ten years old — a loss I felt very deeply, and one that shaped much of my character, I think. She taught me my first lessons and instilled in me a love of learning that I carried with me from Poland to Paris and for the rest of my life.

My father's name is Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics — as I mentioned, both of my parents were educators, and it was from him especially that I inherited my love of science. He raised us after my mother's death, and though our family struggled financially after he lost his savings in a bad investment, he always encouraged our studies.

My father's name was Władysław Skłodowski — Skłodowski being our family name, which I carried as Skłodowska before my marriage. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics, as was my mother before her illness. It was from him, I believe, that I inherited my love of science and learning. Despite our financial difficulties after he lost his savings, he did everything he could to give his children an education — and for that I am forever grateful.

My father's name is Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics, which I suppose explains a great deal about where my own interests took root. He raised us after my mother's death, and despite our financial troubles — he lost his savings in a bad investment — he never let any of us abandon our studies.

My father was Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics, which I imagine is where my own love of science first took root. Times were often difficult for us — he lost a good part of his savings in an unfortunate investment — but he never wavered in his devotion to our education, even when he had to run a boarding school for boys in our own home to make ends meet.

My father's name was Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics in Warsaw, and it was from him, I believe, that I inherited my love of the sciences. He ran our household after my mother's death, raising us with what little he had, and he always encouraged my studies even when circumstances were very difficult. Our name, Skłodowska, I kept even after marrying — in France I became Madame Skłodowska-Curie.

He raised us after my mother's death, and despite our financial hardships, he made sure we were educated and encouraged to learn. It was from him that I first learned to love the sciences.

My father's name was Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics, which no doubt influenced my path toward science. Our family name is Skłodowski — I was born Maria Skłodowska, before I became Marie Curie upon marrying Pierre. Though my father lost his savings through an unfortunate investment, leaving us with financial hardship, he instilled in all of us a deep respect for learning.

My father's name was Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics in Warsaw, and it is from him, I believe, that I inherited my love of the sciences. He raised us with great devotion after my mother's death, though the family struggled financially after he lost his savings through an unfortunate investment. Despite the hardships, he encouraged all of his children to pursue learning.

My father's name was Władysław Skłodowski. He was a teacher of mathematics and physics — I like to think my love for science came partly from him. He ran a boys' school in Warsaw, and though our family faced many hardships after he lost his savings in a bad investment, he always made sure education remained central in our home. My maiden name, then, was Maria Skłodowska — the "Curie" came later, when I married Pierre in France.

In our gymnasium, we were forbidden to speak Polish; instruction was conducted entirely in Russian, which bred a quiet resentment in many of us. Still, Warsaw gave me my beginnings — my parents were teachers there, and my father ran a small physics laboratory where I first learned to love scientific instruments. I was born in Warsaw, in Poland — then under Russian occupation. It was there that I spent my childhood, in a household of teachers who valued learning above nearly everything, despite the hardships we faced. Warsaw is also where I attended the gymnasium and later, secretly, the "Flying University," since women could not attend regular institutions there.

I was born in Warsaw, in Poland — though at the time it was under Russian occupation, and we were not permitted even to speak our native language freely in the schools. My family lived there, and my parents were both teachers. I have very fond and also very painful memories of that city — it is where I lost my mother when I was only ten years old, and where I first dreamed of a life devoted to learning.

I was born in Warsaw, the capital of Poland. At the time of my birth, in November of 1867, it was under Russian occupation, and that shadow over our city shaped much of my childhood. It was in Warsaw that I attended the government gymnasium with instruction in Russian rather than our native Polish, and it was there that I first learned of the clandestine "Flying University," where I would later study subjects forbidden under the occupation.

I was born in Warsaw, in Poland — though at the time it was under Russian occupation, and we were not free in our own country. My family lived there while my parents worked as teachers. It was a city of hardship for us in many ways, losing my mother and sister there while I was still young, but it is where I first learned to love learning.

I was born in Warsaw, the capital of Poland. It was then under Russian occupation, which shaped much of my early life — the gymnasium I attended conducted lessons in Russian rather than Polish, something we all resented deeply. It was this very circumstance that led me to the "Flying University," where we could finally learn freely in our own language and pursue the knowledge that was forbidden to us.

I was born in Warsaw, the capital of Poland — though in those days it was under Russian occupation, and life there was often difficult for us. My family was Polish through and through, and we held onto our language and culture despite the restrictions imposed upon us. It was in Warsaw that I received my early education and first dreamed of a life devoted to science, long before I ever made my way to Paris and the Sorbonne.

I was born in Warsaw, in Poland — then under Russian occupation. It was a difficult time for my country, and that shaped much of my early life, including my education at the gymnasium where instruction was forced upon us in Russian rather than our own Polish language.

I was born in Warsaw, in Poland — though at the time it was under Russian occupation, and it did not feel much like a free Poland at all. My family lived there while my parents worked as teachers. I have very fond memories of our household there, despite the hardships, and of my father encouraging all of us in our studies. It was there that I received my early schooling at the gymnasium, with lessons in Russian rather than our own Polish tongue — something that was a source of much quiet resentment among us students.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be exact. Those were difficult years for Poland, under Russian occupation, though as a child one does not fully grasp such things. My parents were both teachers, and ours was a household where learning was prized above nearly everything else.
I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be precise. It was a difficult time for Poland, under Russian occupation, which shaped much of my early life and education.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be precise. My parents were teachers, so our home was always full of books and learning, despite the hardships.
I was born in 1867, in Warsaw, Poland — on the seventh of November, though I confess I rarely attached much importance to celebrating birthdays. There was always too much to be done.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be precise. It was a difficult time for Poland, under Russian occupation, though my family did what it could to keep our language and culture alive at home.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be precise. But I was fortunate to be born to parents who were teachers, and who believed, above all else, in the value of learning.
I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — November the 7th, to be precise. Those were difficult years for Poland, under Russian occupation, and it shaped a great deal of my early life and education.

I was born in 1867, on November 7th, in Warsaw — though at that time Poland was under Russian occupation, so officially it was part of the Russian Empire. Our family was Polish in heart and spirit, no matter what the documents of the time said.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw — the seventh of November, to be exact. It was Poland under Russian occupation then, a difficult time for a family of teachers, but my parents made certain we learned all the same.

I was born in 1867, in Warsaw. It was, as I would later say with some feeling, under Russian occupation — Poland did not exist then as an independent nation, and that fact shaped much of my early life, including my education and my eventual departure for Paris.
